overview.title: Defining AI: the Dartmouth workshop and 'automating intellectual tasks'
overview.main_topic: The relationship between AI, machine learning and deep learning (figure 1.1), and a definition and brief history of artificial intelligence
overview.central_idea: AI, machine learning and deep learning are nested fields (figure 1.1). AI, born in the 1950s and crystallized at the 1956 Dartmouth workshop, is 'the effort to automate intellectual tasks normally performed by humans' — a broad field that includes machine learning but also approaches that involve no learning at all, such as hardcoded rule systems.
overview.importance: Everything in the book depends on using these three terms precisely. This page fixes the vocabulary and makes the key historical point that for decades AI did not mean learning from data; it meant handcrafting explicit rules — the paradigm (symbolic AI) that machine learning later replaced.
learning_objectives: State the nested relationship between AI, machine learning and deep learning shown in figure 1.1
Give the book's concise definition of AI and explain why it is broader than machine learning
Describe the 1956 Dartmouth workshop proposal and its conjecture about simulating intelligence
Explain why early chess programs with hardcoded rules count as AI but not as machine learning

summary:
The page finishes the chapter's opening sentence with the four questions Chapter 1 will tackle: *What has deep learning achieved so far? How significant is it? Where are we headed next? Should you believe the hype?*

**Section 1.1** states that the first task is to define terms: what are artificial intelligence, machine learning and deep learning, and how do they relate? **Figure 1.1** answers the second question visually with three nested ellipses — *Artificial intelligence* contains *Machine learning*, which contains *Deep learning*.

**Section 1.2** gives a definition and a history of AI. The field was born in the 1950s when computer-science pioneers asked whether computers could be made to "think". The idea crystallized in **1956**, when **John McCarthy**, then a young assistant professor of mathematics at Dartmouth College, organized a summer workshop. Its proposal (quoted in full) rests on the conjecture that *every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it*, and it aims at machines that use language, form abstractions and concepts, solve problems reserved for humans, and improve themselves — all in one summer. The workshop did not solve the riddle, but many attendees became pioneers of the field and it started an intellectual revolution that is still ongoing.

The page then gives the concise definition used throughout the book: **AI is the effort to automate intellectual tasks normally performed by humans.** Because this is so broad, AI contains machine learning and deep learning but also many approaches that involve *no learning at all*. Until the 1980s most AI textbooks did not mention learning; early chess programs consisted only of rules hardcoded by programmers and therefore do not count as machine learning. For a long time most experts believed human-level AI could be reached by handcrafting a large enough set of explicit rules for manipulating knowledge — the sentence continues on p.27, where this approach is named *symbolic AI*.

paragraphs.excerpt: First, we need to define clearly what we're talking about when we mention
paragraphs.what_it_says: Before anything else the authors want precise definitions of artificial intelligence, machine learning and deep learning, and of how they relate to each other; figure 1.1 shows the relationship.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The three terms are often used interchangeably in the media; the book treats them as strictly nested: deep learning is a subset of machine learning, which is a subset of AI. Figure 1.1 draws this as three concentric ellipses with AI outermost.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Getting the nesting right prevents the most common category error in popular writing — equating 'AI' with deep learning or with chatbots. Chapter 20 restates the same nesting in its key-concepts review (p.620).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Set inclusion: $\text{Deep learning} \subset \text{Machine learning} \subset \text{AI}$. Every deep learning system is a machine learning system and an AI system; the converse fails at each step.

terminology.meaning: The outermost field in figure 1.1; defined below as automating intellectual tasks normally performed by humans.
The subfield of AI in which rules are learned from data rather than handcrafted; defined in section 1.3 (p.27–28).
The branch of machine learning based on successive layers of learned representations; defined in section 1.5 (p.31).

paragraphs.excerpt: Artificial intelligence was born in the 1950s, when a handful of pioneers
paragraphs.what_it_says: AI began in the 1950s when a few pioneers of the new field of computer science asked whether computers could be made to 'think' (this paragraph is split by the extractor into e09, e11 and e13 because the figure sits beside it). The authors add that the ramifications of that question are still being explored.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The founding question of AI is not 'can we fit data' but 'can a machine think'. This is a broader and older ambition than anything deep learning currently delivers, which is why the authors say its ramifications are still being explored — Chapter 19 returns to exactly this question (p.588–600).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It places deep learning inside a seventy-year intellectual project rather than treating it as the whole of AI.
connections: p.600: Chapter 19 argues that most of what has been built so far is 'cognitive automation' rather than intelligence in the sense the pioneers meant.

paragraphs.excerpt: While many of the underlying ideas had been brewing in the years and even
paragraphs.what_it_says: Although the ideas had been developing for years, AI became a research field in 1956, when John McCarthy — then a young assistant professor of mathematics at Dartmouth College — organized a summer workshop; its proposal is quoted next.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The 1956 Dartmouth workshop is the conventional birth date of AI as a named discipline. The authors stress that it was a *crystallization* of existing ideas, not a sudden invention.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Knowing that the field is nearly seventy years old helps calibrate the hype discussed later in the chapter: deep learning is the latest of several waves within a long history (see 'Summer can turn to winter', p.38).

terminology.meaning: The summer research project organized by John McCarthy that gave the field its name and founding agenda.

paragraphs.excerpt: The study is to proceed on the basis of the conjecture that every aspect
paragraphs.what_it_says: The quoted Dartmouth proposal: the conjecture that every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate it; the goals of making machines use language, form abstractions and concepts, solve problems now reserved for humans, and improve themselves; and the expectation that a carefully selected group of scientists could make significant progress on one or more of these in a single summer.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Three things stand out. (1) The *conjecture* is a strong claim of computability of intelligence — anything a mind does can be specified precisely enough to simulate. (2) The *agenda* — language, abstraction, problem solving, self-improvement — is essentially the agenda of modern deep learning and generative AI. (3) The *timeline* — one summer — is a striking early example of the over-optimism that the chapter later warns about.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The proposal defines what 'AI' has always meant: a research program about intelligence in general, not any one technique. It also shows that the gap between ambition and delivery has been part of the field since day one.

terminology.meaning: In the proposal, to reproduce a feature of intelligence with a machine given a sufficiently precise description of it.

connections: p.36–38: sections 1.10–1.11 discuss how such optimism led to past AI winters.

paragraphs.excerpt: At the end of the summer, the workshop concluded without having fully solved
paragraphs.what_it_says: The workshop did not solve the problem it set out to investigate, but many attendees became pioneers of the field, and it launched an intellectual revolution that continues today.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The authors judge the workshop by its long-term effect rather than its immediate results — a pattern they will apply to deep learning too: short-term promises may fail while the long-term trajectory holds (p.39, p.621).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It models the kind of judgement the chapter is trying to teach: distinguish an unmet short-term promise from a genuinely important development.
connections: p.621: the same 'hype may recede, impact remains' argument is made about deep learning.

paragraphs.excerpt: Concisely, AI can be described as the effort to automate intellectual tasks
paragraphs.what_it_says: AI is defined as *the effort to automate intellectual tasks normally performed by humans*. This makes it a general field containing machine learning and deep learning but also many approaches with no learning at all. Until the 1980s most AI textbooks did not mention learning; early chess programs used only rules hardcoded by programmers and were not machine learning. For a long time most experts believed human-level AI could be achieved by handcrafting a large enough set of explicit rules for manipulating knowledge (continued on p.27).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The definition is about the *goal* (automating intellectual tasks), not the *method*. A program that plays chess by exhaustively applying programmer-written rules satisfies the goal and is AI, yet nothing in it was learned. Machine learning is defined by a different method — deriving the rules from data — which is why it is a proper subset of AI. The 'handcraft enough rules' belief is the symbolic AI paradigm named on p.27.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the page's key conceptual distinction. Much confusion about what AI can do comes from assuming AI means learning; historically it did not, and the shift from handcrafted rules to learned rules is precisely what section 1.4 (p.28) explains.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Two ways to obtain a program $f$ that maps inputs to answers: (a) a programmer writes the rules of $f$ explicitly (symbolic AI); (b) a learning algorithm searches for $f$ using examples of inputs and desired outputs (machine learning). Both are AI under the book's definition.

terminology.meaning: A task that normally requires human cognition — e.g. playing chess, recognizing an image, translating a sentence.
Decision logic written explicitly by a programmer rather than learned from data.

connections: p.27: the handcrafted-rules approach is named symbolic AI, dominant from the 1950s to the late 1980s and peaking in the expert systems boom.
p.28: section 1.4 contrasts classical programming (rules + data → answers) with machine learning (data + answers → rules).
p.620: Chapter 20 gives the same definition, 'all attempts to automate human cognitive processes'.

concepts.name: Artificial intelligence (AI)
concepts.definition: The effort to automate intellectual tasks normally performed by humans (book's definition on this page).
concepts.intuition: If a computer does something that would require thinking if a person did it — playing chess, translating, recognizing faces — that is AI, regardless of how the program was produced.
concepts.technical: AI is defined by its goal, not its technique. It includes rule-based (symbolic) systems with no learning, classical machine learning, and deep learning. Figure 1.1 shows it as the outermost of three nested ellipses.
concepts.significance: Because AI is so broad, statements about 'AI' are often really statements about one specific sub-approach; the book's precise usage avoids that confusion.
concepts.example: An early chess program whose moves are chosen by rules written entirely by programmers is AI but not machine learning.
concepts.misconception: That AI necessarily involves learning from data. Until the 1980s most AI textbooks did not mention learning at all.

concepts.name: Machine learning (as a subfield of AI)
concepts.definition: The subfield of AI in which the rules for a task are learned from data rather than handcrafted; shown in figure 1.1 as a subset of AI that itself contains deep learning.
concepts.intuition: Instead of a programmer writing the rules, the computer is shown examples and works out the rules itself.
concepts.technical: This page only positions machine learning inside AI; its definition and the contrast with classical programming are developed in sections 1.3–1.4 (p.27–30).
concepts.significance: It is the method that replaced symbolic AI when handcrafted rules proved intractable for fuzzy problems such as image classification (p.27).
concepts.example: A spam filter that learns which words indicate spam from thousands of labelled emails, rather than from a programmer's list.
concepts.misconception: That machine learning and AI are the same thing; machine learning is one approach among several within AI.

concepts.name: Deep learning (as a subfield of machine learning)
concepts.definition: The innermost ellipse of figure 1.1: a branch of machine learning. Its defining feature — successive layers of learned representations — is explained in section 1.5 (p.31).
concepts.intuition: Deep learning is a specific way of doing machine learning, which is itself a specific way of doing AI.
concepts.technical: On this page deep learning appears only in the figure; the book later characterizes it as models built from chains of geometric transformations organized in layers (p.31, p.620).
concepts.significance: It is the technique responsible for the current wave of AI progress and the subject of the rest of the book.
concepts.example: An image classifier made of stacked convolutional layers trained end-to-end on labelled photos.
concepts.misconception: That 'deep learning' and 'AI' are interchangeable; deep learning is the smallest of the three nested fields.

concepts.name: Symbolic AI (handcrafted rules)
concepts.definition: The approach of achieving intelligence by having programmers handcraft a sufficiently large set of explicit rules for manipulating knowledge; named 'symbolic AI' on p.27.
concepts.intuition: Write down everything an expert knows as if-then rules and let the computer apply them.
concepts.technical: Rules and knowledge are explicit symbols manipulated by logic; no parameters are fitted to data. Early chess programs are the book's example.
concepts.significance: It was the dominant AI paradigm from the 1950s to the late 1980s (p.27) and is the baseline against which machine learning is defined.
concepts.example: A chess program that evaluates positions with programmer-written heuristics and searches moves by fixed rules.
concepts.misconception: That symbolic AI is not 'real' AI. Under the book's definition it is, because it automates an intellectual task; it simply does not learn.

deeper.title: Goal versus method: why the three ellipses nest
deeper.body:
The three terms are defined at different levels:

- **AI** is defined by a *goal*: automate intellectual tasks normally performed by humans. Any method counts.
- **Machine learning** is defined by a *method*: obtain the task's rules from data instead of writing them by hand (p.28). It pursues the AI goal, so it sits inside AI.
- **Deep learning** is defined by a *specific family of methods* within machine learning: learn the rules as a stack of successive representations (p.31). It is therefore inside machine learning.

This is why figure 1.1 is drawn as nested ellipses rather than as three separate circles or a Venn diagram with partial overlaps: each inner field satisfies the definition of the outer one by construction. Note (not in the book): the diagram says nothing about relative *size* or *importance* — the inner ellipse is drawn smaller only because it is the most specific category.

deeper.title: Reading the Dartmouth proposal against today's systems
deeper.body:
Beyond the book: it is instructive to line the 1956 goals up with what the book will cover.

| Dartmouth goal (1956) | Where the book treats it |
|---|---|
| make machines use language | text models and Transformers (Chapters on text and generative AI; section 1.8 'The age of generative AI', p.35) |
| form abstractions and concepts | learned representations in successive layers (sections 1.4–1.6, p.28–34) |
| solve problems now reserved for humans | the achievements list in 1.9 (p.35) |
| improve themselves | the training loop that adjusts weights from feedback (1.6, p.32–34) |

The proposal's optimism about doing this 'together for a summer' is the ancestor of the hype the chapter warns about in 1.10 (p.36). Chapter 19 (p.600) argues that even today's systems mostly deliver *cognitive automation* rather than the general intelligence the proposal imagined.

deeper.title: A chess program with no learning
deeper.body: Picture a chess program from the 1960s. Its programmer writes an evaluation function by hand — 'a queen is worth 9 pawns, a rook 5, a knight on the rim is worth less' — plus a procedure that looks several moves ahead and picks the best-scoring line. Every piece of chess knowledge was typed in by a human. The program is unquestionably AI by the book's definition (it automates an intellectual task humans do), but it has never looked at a single example game and would play identically no matter how many games it lost. Contrast a modern system that adjusts its evaluation from millions of games: that is machine learning. The difference is not what the program does but **where its rules came from**.

misconceptions.claim: AI means computers that learn from data.
misconceptions.correction: Learning is one approach within AI. The book defines AI by its goal — automating intellectual tasks normally performed by humans — and notes that until the 1980s most AI textbooks did not mention learning at all. Rule-based chess programs are AI without being machine learning.

misconceptions.claim: Deep learning, machine learning and AI are three names for the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Figure 1.1 shows them as strictly nested: deep learning is a subset of machine learning, which is a subset of AI. Each inner term is more specific.

misconceptions.claim: AI is a recent invention that appeared with chatbots.
misconceptions.correction: The field was born in the 1950s and crystallized at the 1956 Dartmouth workshop organized by John McCarthy; its founding question — can computers think — is still being explored.

earlier.note: Chapter opener; the opening sentence completed here begins there.

later.note: The handcrafted-rules approach is named symbolic AI; its limits on fuzzy problems lead to machine learning (section 1.3).
Section 1.4 contrasts classical programming with machine learning and explains learning rules from data.
Section 1.5 defines what is 'deep' in deep learning.
Sections 1.11–1.12 on AI winters and the long-term promise, echoing the Dartmouth over-optimism.
Chapter 19 revisits the founding question of AI and argues current systems are 'cognitive automation'.
Chapter 20 restates the AI / machine learning / deep learning nesting.

related_figures.note: Figure 1.1: three nested ellipses — artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning.

takeaways: AI, machine learning and deep learning are nested: deep learning ⊂ machine learning ⊂ AI (figure 1.1).
AI is the effort to automate intellectual tasks normally performed by humans — a definition about the goal, not the method.

AI was born in the 1950s and crystallized at the 1956 Dartmouth workshop organized by John McCarthy, whose proposal conjectured that every feature of intelligence could be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate it.
For decades AI did not involve learning at all: early chess programs used hardcoded rules, and most experts expected human-level AI from a large enough set of handcrafted rules (symbolic AI, p.27).

questions.question: According to figure 1.1, which statement about the relationship between the three fields is correct?
options: Deep learning is a subset of machine learning, which is a subset of artificial intelligence
Machine learning is a subset of deep learning, which is a subset of artificial intelligence
Artificial intelligence is a subset of machine learning
The three fields overlap partially but none contains another
questions.answer: Deep learning is a subset of machine learning, which is a subset of artificial intelligence
questions.explanation: Figure 1.1 draws three nested ellipses with artificial intelligence outermost, machine learning inside it, and deep learning innermost. The second option reverses the inner two; the third reverses the whole order; the fourth describes a Venn diagram with partial overlaps, which is not what the figure shows.

questions.question: Give the book's concise definition of artificial intelligence.
questions.answer: The effort to automate intellectual tasks normally performed by humans.
questions.explanation: This is the definition given verbatim in the last paragraph of the page. It is deliberately about the goal rather than any particular technique, which is why AI includes approaches that involve no learning.

questions.question: Why does an early chess program made of hardcoded rules qualify as AI but not as machine learning?
questions.answer: It automates an intellectual task humans perform (playing chess), so it fits the definition of AI; but all of its rules were written by programmers rather than learned from data, so it is not machine learning.
questions.explanation: The page says AI 'includes many more approaches that may not involve any learning' and gives early chess programs as the example: they 'only involved hardcoded rules crafted by programmers and didn't qualify as machine learning'. The distinction is where the rules come from, not what the program does.

questions.question: Which of the following was NOT among the goals stated in the 1956 Dartmouth workshop proposal?
options: Make machines form abstractions and concepts
Make machines learn from large labelled datasets
questions.answer: Make machines learn from large labelled datasets
questions.explanation: The quoted proposal lists using language, forming abstractions and concepts, solving kinds of problems now reserved for humans, and improving themselves. Learning from large labelled datasets is the modern machine learning method; it is not mentioned in the proposal, consistent with the page's point that early AI was not centred on learning.

questions.question: Who organized the 1956 workshop at which AI crystallized as a field, and what was his position at the time?
questions.answer: John McCarthy, then a young Assistant Professor of Mathematics at Dartmouth College.
questions.explanation: The page states this directly when describing how 'artificial intelligence' crystallized as a field of research in 1956.

questions.question: The Dartmouth proposal expected significant progress 'if a carefully selected group of scientists work on it together for a summer', and the workshop ended without solving its riddle. How do the authors nonetheless evaluate it, and what does this suggest about how they will evaluate deep learning later in the chapter?
questions.answer: They judge it by its long-term effect: it produced many pioneers and 'set in motion an intellectual revolution that is still ongoing'. This foreshadows their stance on deep learning — short-term hype and unmet promises can coexist with a genuine long-term revolution (sections 1.10–1.12).
questions.explanation: The paragraph after the quote explicitly separates the unmet immediate goal from the lasting impact. The same reasoning is used on p.39 and p.621, where the authors argue that the hype around deep learning may recede while its sustained impact remains.

questions.question: Can you explain, without looking, why the statement 'until the 1980s most AI textbooks didn't mention learning' is consistent with the book's definition of AI?
questions.answer: Because AI is defined by the goal of automating intellectual tasks, not by learning. The dominant method for decades was handcrafting explicit rules (symbolic AI), which needs no learning at all.
questions.explanation: Self-check on the page's central distinction between goal (AI) and method (learning). If you found yourself assuming AI implies learning, re-read the last paragraph of the page and the opening of p.27.
